title: South Wales Police's Operator Initiated Facial Recognition app identifies a 38-year-old in Cardiff wanted on a 2012 European arrest warrant from Poland; he is remanded to Westminster magistrates
summary: A South Wales Police officer's OIFR phone app matched a 38-year-old in Cardiff to a 2012 Polish European arrest warrant for drug dealing and assaulting an officer; he was remanded (July 2025).
account: South Wales Police and Gwent Police are the first UK forces with the Operator Initiated Facial Recognition (OIFR) app. It lets an officer photograph a person on a police phone and compare the image with a reference database. It is for when the person refuses or gives false details. It launched in December 2024. More than 500 officers had been trained by July 2025 (Emergency Services Times, 15 July 2025). In one use, an officer in Cardiff identified a 38-year-old man wanted on a European arrest warrant since 2012. The warrant was for drug dealing and assaulting a police officer with a weapon in Poland. He was remanded in custody to Westminster magistrates' court (Wales Online, 14 July 2025). The forces report 50 South Wales searches producing 10 arrests, and six Gwent uses with three matches and one arrest. They cite National Physical Laboratory testing in which the correct match came top for people in the database (Wales Online). The arrest date is not given.
purpose: Built to confirm the identity of a person an officer suspects is missing, at risk or wanted when they cannot or will not give details. This identification was that use.
system: Operator Initiated Facial Recognition (OIFR) mobile app, South Wales Police and Gwent Police
segment: Street identity checks of people who refuse or give false details

ratings.reason: South Wales Police identified in Cardiff a man wanted on a 2012 European arrest warrant and remanded him. It reports 10 arrests from 50 app searches. A measurable result for the forces, on their own figures as relayed by the press.

One man wanted for drug dealing and assaulting an officer with a weapon in Poland was taken into custody for extradition proceedings. The reports give no further harm prevented. So the public benefit is the execution of a warrant.

ai_role.statement: The app compared a photograph taken on a police phone to the reference database and returned the match that identified the man. Officers then confirmed the warrant and detained him. The force says National Physical Laboratory testing found the correct match returned as the top result for persons in the database. It says the app returns nothing for people not in it. Neither report names the vendor, the algorithm or a match score. Both rest on the force's figures.
